paper.title: Freeform Preference Learning for Robotic Manipulation
paper.source_version: arXiv v3, submitted 2026-08-01 01:25:23 UTC and verified as the latest public revision on 2026-08-30; PDF SHA-256 3abfaaa7a63a8d63b7e9fae2e208b84617c2d05042d2cf260d637e6996769ffe; TeX-source SHA-256 b7106307738be0ae6a7e05d6407095053afe350827bf0d77bb1387cf9ce67b03; official method repository commit dfb62a85374d6cd6d312ab86b7fa030161da0ce9, official real-world collection repository commit 17cffe62d4c0dc3474a3bc1ae221046cf839c129, and official project-page repository commit 8aac1a63be52a832a1f9adbde2809af3fa3cbc59, checked 2026-08-30

decision_relevance.why_admitted: FPL supplies a concrete human-steering schema—freeform natural-language axes plus per-axis trajectory preferences—and a learned vector-valued reward representation. It directly informs how Sam could elicit and version task-reward components and keep their objective evaluations separate. Its policy result is also a sharp fixed-trainer boundary: FPL relabels trajectories and fine-tunes a policy that consumes axis-score conditioning, so the reported gain is not evidence for swapping only an executable task reward into Sam's unchanged controller/trainer.
not_evidence_for: reference-motion selection, ordering, composition, transition guards, recovery, or certification
an executable per-step task reward consumed by an otherwise unchanged trainer
a task-reward-only improvement under fixed policy observations, architecture, data, and optimization
compatibility with a frozen controller that does not already consume an axis-score conditioning vector
test-time reference-oracle steering; FPL changes reward-conditioning values supplied to its trained policy
objective validation or safety of the learned VLM reward outside the reported tasks and data distribution
automatic selection of safe, in-distribution target reward values at test time
variable-axis policy conditioning at test time; the evaluated policy uses a selected fixed axis set
a complete reproducible match between the paper recipe and the released launch scripts

mechanisms.name: Freeform per-axis trajectory preferences
mechanisms.description: An annotator views two complete trajectories, supplies or uses one or more natural-language judgment axes, and records A-versus-B preference separately for each axis. The number of axes may vary by pair; the implementation also permits equivalence, which the paper's training recipe drops.

mechanisms.name: Language-conditioned trajectory reward model
mechanisms.description: One reward model receives a trajectory and a natural-language axis and returns an axis-specific scalar. Pairwise supervision uses a Bradley-Terry loss, while the proposed trajectory score is the sum of multimodal-transformer scores over observation prefixes.

mechanisms.name: Multi-axis reward-conditioned policy extraction
mechanisms.description: A representative fixed set of axes is chosen, every trajectory is labeled with its reward-model score on every selected axis, and a policy is trained by action log-likelihood conditioned on state plus the complete axis-score list. At test time, changing desired normalized scores steers the already trained policy.

mechanisms.name: Iterative preference-and-rollout loop
mechanisms.description: Across iterations, preferences accumulate, the reward model and conditioned policy are retrained, the new policy generates rollouts, and those rollouts expand the training dataset. Human axes may shift from coarse completion criteria to finer quality criteria as behavior improves.

failure_modes.name: Manual target selection and fixed policy axes
failure_modes.description: The reward model is unbounded, target values must remain behaviorally effective and in distribution, and the current policy consumes a selected fixed axis set. The authors identify automatic target selection and variable-axis policies as future work.

failure_modes.name: Not a drop-in fixed-trainer task reward
failure_modes.description: FPL scores complete trajectories offline, changes the policy input to include all axis-score pairs, fine-tunes the policy, and can expand the replay dataset. Applying the full mechanism to Sam would therefore change frozen trainer/controller and data contracts unless those interfaces were predeclared and held fixed.

failure_modes.name: Reward validity is evaluated qualitatively
failure_modes.description: The dense-credit claim is illustrated on one representative setup-table rollout, while v3 reports neither held-out reward-model accuracy nor calibration, adversarial optimization, out-of-distribution, or reward-hacking tests. Policy outcomes therefore do not independently validate the reward signal itself.

failure_modes.name: Real-world metric-definition ambiguity
failure_modes.description: The appendix calls the per-task quantity success rate, while the official project page calls the aggregate average task progress. V3 does not give a complete scoring rubric or blind-rating protocol for each qualitative task, so the 38-point headline cannot be reconstructed from the paper alone.

failure_modes.name: Human-annotation and uncertainty limits
failure_modes.description: Preference collection remains more costly than unsupervised learning. V3 gives per-label timing and label counts but no annotator count, agreement, demographic protocol, or repeated reward/policy training seeds for real-world tasks; real-world uncertainty comes from 20 rollouts per method.

failure_modes.name: Z-score conditioning is not bounded
failure_modes.description: Appendix 9.2 says per-axis standardization makes rewards bounded, but the stated transform (r-mean)/standard deviation is unbounded. Rounding to one decimal discretizes values without providing an admissible range or clipping rule.

failure_modes.name: Pinned public launchers do not match the paper recipe
failure_modes.description: At the reviewed commit, the reward launcher selects the non-cumulative qwen_open model for one epoch with stride 10, while v3 describes summed prefix scores, per-task strides, and checkpoint selection within 500 epochs. The invoked pi05_droid_finetune preset uses 60,000 steps rather than the paper's 30,000, and the environment installs mutable Transformers main. The repository is useful but not an exact evaluation manifest.

evaluation.name: Four-task real-world policy comparison
evaluation.description: On 20 rollouts per method, FPL reports per-task means of 0.94, 0.70, 0.55, and 0.81 and an average of 0.75 plus or minus 0.04. The best baseline average is Filtered BC at 0.37 plus or minus 0.04, giving the reported 0.38 absolute gap.

evaluation.name: Robomimic-based simulation comparison
evaluation.description: Across three seeds, FPL reports object-rearrangement success 0.84 plus or minus 0.09 and bimodal-square throughput 1.19 plus or minus 0.01, exceeding all listed baselines; the inverted conditioning yields throughput 1.24 plus or minus 0.01.

evaluation.name: Behavior compositionality and same-policy steering tests
evaluation.description: The bimodal dataset contains fast and slow left-peg trajectories but only slow right-peg trajectories. FPL produces faster right-peg behavior and, with changed score conditioning, the same policy reaches 1.00 success in both normal and inverted peg directions; the real cube task changes target-bowl score prompts to steer placement.

evaluation.name: Qualitative temporal credit-assignment comparison
evaluation.description: On one setup-table rollout, selected FPL axes peak around corresponding placement events without explicit subtask boundaries, whereas the single binary-preference reward has a late spike with no major completion event. The paper presents this as qualitative, not calibrated, evidence.

evaluation.name: Preference diversity and time-per-label analysis
evaluation.description: Plate-toast collection yields 295 trajectory pairs, over 1,477 axis-level comparisons, and 41 distinct labels. Sharing video-viewing cost across several labels is reported as about 1.85 times faster per label than single-preference annotation.

evidence.locator: Title, authors, submission history, DOI, v3 PDF and TeX-source links; exact downloaded bytes verified 2026-08-30
evidence.claim: V3 is the latest public revision as of the corpus date; it was submitted 1 August 2026. The reviewed 24-page PDF and TeX archive have the recorded SHA-256 digests.

FPL compares full trajectories, permits predefined or annotator-written natural-language axes with variable K_ij, and trains one axis-conditioned scalar reward using the summed Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood.
The proposed trajectory reward is a sum of axis-conditioned prefix scores from a multimodal transformer over observation history.

evidence.locator: Section 3.2, Eq. 5 and offline/online policy-extraction discussion
evidence.claim: FPL selects representative axes, labels each trajectory with all axis rewards, and trains a policy by action log-likelihood conditioned on state and the axis-score list; the procedure can be offline or repeated with new rollouts.
The iterative loop accumulates preferences, retrains reward and policy models, adds current-policy rollouts to D, and allows the selected axis set and human criteria to evolve.

evidence.locator: End of Section 3.2; Appendix Section 9.2; Section 6
evidence.claim: At test time the policy is steered by target per-axis rewards. Rewards are standardized over D because raw outputs are unbounded; appropriate target selection and variable-axis policies remain future work.

Evaluation spans four Franka/DROID real-world tasks with wrist and third-person cameras plus joint-velocity control and two Robomimic-based simulation tasks; results use 20 real-world rollouts per method and three simulation seeds with mean and standard error.
The complete per-task real-world table reports FPL means 0.94/0.70/0.55/0.81 and average 0.75 plus or minus 0.04 versus best-baseline average 0.37 plus or minus 0.04, an absolute 0.38 gap.

The simulation tables report all baseline means and standard errors, including FPL object-rearrangement success 0.84 plus or minus 0.09, normal/inverted throughput 1.19/1.24, and 1.00 success in both bimodal directions.
The same multi-axis-conditioned policy composes fast right-peg behavior absent from demonstrations and is steered to the inverted peg or a commanded bowl by changing target reward conditioning.
A representative setup-table rollout qualitatively shows temporally localized FPL axis rewards without subtask labels and a late erroneous spike for the single binary-preference reward.

evidence.locator: Appendix Tables 2-3; Section 8 and Figures 9-10; Section 5.3
evidence.claim: The paper reports all task dataset counts and interface semantics, about 1.85x lower time per freeform label, and plate-toast diversity of 295 pairs, over 1,477 axis judgments, and 41 distinct labels; annotator count and agreement are not reported.

The real-world reward implementation uses the paper-labelled Qwen 3.5 VL 4B, two camera streams, causal history, a frozen vision encoder, full fine-tuning elsewhere, per-timestep linear scores summed over time, validation selection within 500 epochs, task-specific strides, sequence length 20, batch 32, LR 1e-5, 128-square images, and drops equivalent labels.

Real policy training z-scores rewards, rounds to one decimal, full-fine-tunes pi_0.5 for 30,000 steps with batch 32, action chunk 16 and eight executed actions; simulation uses fixed reward heads, float conditioning plus 0.2 noise; reported compute is one H100 and generally RTX 4500 simulation GPUs.

Baselines change reward dimensionality, supervision source, dataset filtering, or policy extraction; no reported arm substitutes only an executable task reward while holding the complete trainer/controller contract fixed.
The authors report human-preference cost, manual target-reward selection, and the fixed policy-axis set as limitations.
